# Wang et al. (2026), section 3.2, Experiment 1 (N = 123).
# Outcome is NS+: category paired with a rewarded originally CHOSEN item.
# Unchosen-item inference predicts OR < 1; do not reverse this label.
# Published central estimates and 95% HPD intervals are entered without
# reconstructing individual-level data from rounded odds ratios.
original_n <- 123L
original <- tibble(
  pair_type = c("chosen", "unchosen"),
  odds_ratio = c(2.01, 0.69),
  lower = c(1.46, 0.52), upper = c(2.79, 0.91), N = original_n
)

# Aggregate-only reproduction of original Rmd preprocessing/power calculation.
# The source Rmd's section "Power analysis for Exp 2" operates on Exp1 data.
original_summary <- fromJSON("original-exp1-summary.json")
stopifnot(original_summary$reproduced_model_n == 123L,
          original_summary$reproduced_model_trials == 5892L)
original_d <- abs(original_summary$unchosen_cohens_d)

```{r}
#| label: analysis-functions
#| code-summary: "Show the analysis code (shared by Phase 1 and Phase 2)"
#| cache: true
#| cache.extra: !expr list(ids = c(experiment_id, experiment_id_phase2), hashes = tools::md5sum(analysis_input_files[file.exists(analysis_input_files)]), rstanarm = as.character(packageVersion("rstanarm")))
# Source: OSF xjhkf, Experiment_1_analysis.Rmd, revised main model
# ("Edit of the main model by Xinyue") and separate chosen/unchosen models.
# Source-code preprocessing, including 300 < rating RT < 8000 ms, category
# means rounded to 2 decimals, and absolute separately z-scored left/right
# means, is reproduced. This differs from the paper's signed-difference prose.
as_bool <- function(x) tolower(as.character(x)) %in% "true"
score_attention_checks <- function(trials) {
  attention <- trials |> filter(task == "attention_check")
  if (!nrow(attention)) return(tibble(
    participant_id = character(), n_attention_checks = integer(),
    n_attention_correct = integer(), n_attention_nonresponses = integer(),
    attention_accuracy = double(), attention_nonresponse_rate = double(),
    exclude_attention_accuracy = logical(), exclude_attention_nonresponses = logical()))
  attention |>
    mutate(attention_nonresponse = is.na(response) | response == "" |
             tolower(response) == "null",
           attention_correct = !attention_nonresponse & !is.na(letter) &
             tolower(response) == tolower(letter)) |>
    group_by(participant_id) |>
    summarise(n_attention_checks = n(),
              n_attention_correct = sum(attention_correct),
              n_attention_nonresponses = sum(attention_nonresponse), .groups = "drop") |>
    mutate(attention_accuracy = n_attention_correct / n_attention_checks,
           attention_nonresponse_rate = n_attention_nonresponses / n_attention_checks,
           exclude_attention_accuracy = attention_accuracy < 0.10,
           exclude_attention_nonresponses = attention_nonresponse_rate > 0.90)
}
read_phase <- function(id) {
  dir <- file.path("..", "data", "raw", id)
  if (!all(file.exists(file.path(dir, c("participants.csv", "trials.csv"))))) return(NULL)
  read_export <- function(name) read_csv(file.path(dir, name),
    col_types = cols(.default = col_character()), show_col_types = FALSE)
  participants <- read_export("participants.csv") |>
    mutate(completed = as_bool(completed), practice_misses = as.numeric(practice_misses))
  trials <- read_export("trials.csv")
  errors <- if (file.exists(file.path(dir, "errors.csv"))) read_export("errors.csv") else tibble()
  # Decision fixed on 2026-10-27 while Pilot B was underway, before full-sample
  # collection. Exp1 paper: three missed practice responses. Exp1 source code
  # counts <10% attention accuracy / >90% nonresponses without removing them;
  # Exp2 source code applies those thresholds. This replication applies them.
  # Denominators include ALL presented letter checks; misses are incorrect.
  # A participant with no presented checks is not excluded on attention grounds.
  attention <- score_attention_checks(trials)
  participants <- participants |> left_join(attention, by = "participant_id") |>
    mutate(across(c(n_attention_checks, n_attention_correct, n_attention_nonresponses),
                  ~ coalesce(.x, 0L)),
           across(c(exclude_attention_accuracy, exclude_attention_nonresponses),
                  ~ coalesce(.x, FALSE)))
  complete <- participants |> filter(completed)
  # Completed export flag replaces the original platform's nonempty unique_code.
  # Keep the original stopping criterion; no memory-accuracy cutoff is added.
  keep <- complete |> filter(!as_bool(qa_run), !as_bool(preview_run),
                             coalesce(practice_misses, 0) < 3,
                             !exclude_attention_accuracy, !exclude_attention_nonresponses)
  retained <- trials |> filter(participant_id %in% keep$participant_id)
  ratings <- retained |> filter(task == "preference_rating") |>
    mutate(rt = as.numeric(rt), rating = as.numeric(rating)) |>
    filter(rt > 300, rt < 8000) |>
    group_by(participant_id, category) |>
    summarise(mean_rating = round(mean(rating, na.rm = TRUE), 2), .groups = "drop")
  choices <- retained |> filter(task == "final_choice") |>
    mutate(rt = as.numeric(rt), timed_out = as_bool(timed_out),
      p_ns = if_else(timed_out, NA_integer_, as.integer(as_bool(chose_paired_reward))),
      chosen_trial_centered = as.integer(pair_type == "unchosen")) |>
    left_join(ratings |> rename(Left_mean_ratings = mean_rating),
      by = c("participant_id", "left_category" = "category")) |>
    left_join(ratings |> rename(Right_mean_ratings = mean_rating),
      by = c("participant_id", "right_category" = "category")) |>
    group_by(participant_id) |>
    mutate(z_score_norm_drate_by_outcome = abs(as.numeric(scale(Left_mean_ratings)) -
                                               as.numeric(scale(Right_mean_ratings)))) |>
    ungroup()
  # A missed choice is missing, never silently interpreted as a right choice.
  # Missing final-choice responses are excluded consistently across exports.
  model_data <- choices |> filter(!is.na(p_ns), is.finite(z_score_norm_drate_by_outcome)) |>
    mutate(pid = factor(participant_id))
  list(participants = participants, trials = trials, errors = errors, attention = attention,
    complete = complete, keep = keep, retained = retained, choices = choices,
    model_data = model_data,
    n_no_response = sum(vapply(split(choices$timed_out, choices$participant_id), all, logical(1))))
}

fit_source_model <- function(data, formula) {
  # Original analysis: normal(0,2.5), decov(regularization=1), seed123,
  # four chains, 4000 iterations, first2000 warmup, random participant intercept.
  fit <- rstanarm::stan_glmer(formula = formula, data = data,
    family = binomial(link = "logit"),
    prior = rstanarm::normal(0, 2.5),
    prior_intercept = rstanarm::normal(0, 2.5),
    prior_covariance = rstanarm::decov(regularization = 1),
    chains = 4, iter = 4000, warmup = 2000, seed = 123, refresh = 0)
  sampler <- rstan::get_sampler_params(fit$stanfit, inc_warmup = FALSE)
  divergent <- sum(vapply(sampler, function(s) sum(s[, "divergent__"]), numeric(1)))
  if (divergent > 0) {
    # Diagnostic-only sampler adjustment; formula/priors/chains/iterations unchanged.
    # The first source-default pilot fit had2 divergences in the chosen-only model.
    fit <- update(fit, adapt_delta = 0.99, refresh = 0)
    attr(fit, "tolerance_tightened") <- TRUE
  }
  fit
}
fit_phase <- function(d) {
  if (is.null(d) || n_distinct(d$model_data$pid) < 2) return(NULL)
  x <- d$model_data
  if (!all(c("chosen", "unchosen") %in% x$pair_type)) return(NULL)
  fits <- list(
    main = fit_source_model(x,
      p_ns ~ chosen_trial_centered * z_score_norm_drate_by_outcome + (1 | pid)),
    chosen = fit_source_model(filter(x, pair_type == "chosen"),
      p_ns ~ z_score_norm_drate_by_outcome + (1 | pid)),
    unchosen = fit_source_model(filter(x, pair_type == "unchosen"),
      p_ns ~ z_score_norm_drate_by_outcome + (1 | pid)))
  attr(fits, "N") <- n_distinct(x$pid)
  fits
}
or_summary <- function(fit, term = "(Intercept)") {
  draws <- as.matrix(fit)[, term]
  hpdi <- coda::HPDinterval(coda::mcmc(draws), prob = 0.95)[1, ]
  tibble(odds_ratio = exp(median(draws)), lower = exp(hpdi[1]), upper = exp(hpdi[2]),
    posterior_probability_below_one = mean(draws < 0))
}
model_summary <- function(fits) {
  if (is.null(fits)) return(tibble())
  bind_rows(or_summary(fits$chosen) |> mutate(pair_type = "chosen"),
            or_summary(fits$unchosen) |> mutate(pair_type = "unchosen")) |>
    mutate(N = attr(fits, "N"))
}
diagnostics <- function(fits) {
  if (is.null(fits)) return(tibble())
  imap_dfr(fits, function(fit, name) {
    summary <- summary(fit, probs = c(0.025, 0.975))
    sampler <- rstan::get_sampler_params(fit$stanfit, inc_warmup = FALSE)
    tibble(Model = name, `Maximum Rhat` = max(summary[, "Rhat"], na.rm = TRUE),
      `Minimum effective N` = min(summary[, "n_eff"], na.rm = TRUE),
      Divergences = sum(vapply(sampler, function(s) sum(s[, "divergent__"]), numeric(1))),
      `Sampler tolerance tightened` = isTRUE(attr(fit, "tolerance_tightened")))
  })
}
comparison_plot <- function(...) {
  studies <- list(...)
  studies <- studies[!map_lgl(studies, ~ is.null(.x) || nrow(.x) == 0)]
  plotted <- imap_dfr(studies, ~ mutate(.x, Study = .y)) |>
    mutate(Study = factor(Study, levels = names(studies)),
      pair_type = factor(pair_type, levels = c("chosen", "unchosen")))
  ggplot(plotted, aes(x = pair_type, y = odds_ratio, ymin = lower, ymax = upper)) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
    geom_pointrange(colour = "#1E6E76") + scale_y_log10() +
    facet_wrap(~Study, nrow = 1) +
    labs(x = "Category-pair type", y = "Odds of choosing NS+ (log scale)") +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
}
phase1 <- read_phase(experiment_id)
phase2 <- read_phase(experiment_id_phase2)
have_data <- !is.null(phase1)
have_phase2 <- !is.null(phase2)
phase1_fits <- fit_phase(phase1)
phase2_fits <- fit_phase(phase2)
phase1_estimates <- model_summary(phase1_fits)
phase2_estimates <- model_summary(phase2_fits)
format_hpdi <- function(lower, upper) ifelse(is.na(lower) | is.na(upper), "Not available",
  paste0("[", formatC(lower, format = "g", digits = 3), ", ", formatC(upper, format = "g", digits = 3), "]"))
```

```{r}
#| label: key-stats
#| echo: false
# The summary, addendum, and Results share the same excluded Phase 1 data.
key_phase1_data <- phase1
key_phase1_n <- if (is.null(phase1)) NA_integer_ else n_distinct(phase1$model_data$pid)
key_phase1_estimates <- phase1_estimates

key_row <- function(study, estimates, n, collected) {
  if (!collected) {
    return(tibble(Study = study, N = "not yet collected", OR = "not yet collected", `95% HPDI` = ""))
  }
  if (!nrow(estimates)) {
    return(tibble(Study = study, N = as.character(n), OR = "not estimable", `95% HPDI` = ""))
  }
  estimates |> filter(pair_type == "unchosen") |>
    transmute(Study = study, N = as.character(N),
              OR = formatC(odds_ratio, format = "f", digits = 3),
              `95% HPDI` = format_hpdi(lower, upper))
}
key_rows <- bind_rows(
  key_row("Original", original, original_n, TRUE),
  key_row("Phase 1: replication (Pilot B)", key_phase1_estimates, key_phase1_n, !is.null(key_phase1_data)),
  key_row("Phase 2: extension", phase2_estimates,
          if (is.null(phase2)) NA_integer_ else n_distinct(phase2$model_data$pid), !is.null(phase2))
)
key_rows |> knitr::kable(caption = "Unchosen-category model intercept: odds of choosing the category paired with a rewarded chosen item. OR below1 indicates the predicted inverse preference. Original: Wang et al. (2026), section3.2; Pilot B: posterior median OR and exponentiated log-odds HPDI.")
```

# Phase 1: Replication

## Introduction

I’m interested in how memory and decision-making interact to support adaptive behavior, including how information from past experiences can guide decisions in novel situations. Wang et al. (2026) found that value inferred for an unchosen option generalized to novel objects within the same semantic category. I would like to specifically replicate the finding that participants preferred novel items that were semantically similar to an unchosen option whose chosen counterpart received no reward over novel items related to an unchosen option whose chosen counterpart was rewarded, because it suggested how we generalize value beyond direct experience to make adaptive decisions.

The original study used 128 object images, with 16 from each of eight semantic categories in the DinoLab Object Database. Participants were asked to repeatedly choose one item from each pair that they predicted would be more valuable and justify their decisions during deliberation phase. They then learned whether the chosen items received a reward or no reward during outcome learning phase. In the final decision phase, they chose between novel exemplars from all categories to test whether previously learned and inferred value of unchosen options generalized to novel objects from the same semantic categories. A surprise memory test of item and associative memory was conducted to understand the relationship between memory for original associations and novel decisions.

The key statistical test was a multilevel Bayesian logistic regression testing whether participants’ selection of novel items depended on whether the corresponding previously seen unchosen item had been paired with a chosen item that received a reward or no reward.

## Methods

### Power analysis

```{r}
#| label: power
# Source Exp1 Rmd lines925-946: one-sample, two-sided t-test against0.5
# on participant-level unchosen NS+ proportions; Cohen d=t/sqrt(N).
# This is the authors' planning approximation, NOT power for stan_glmer.
# Basis is original data only, never the three-person pilot effect.
power_rows <- map_dfr(c(0.80, 0.90, 0.95), function(pw) {
  out <- pwr::pwr.t.test(d = original_d, sig.level = 0.05, power = pw,
                       type = "one.sample", alternative = "two.sided")
  tibble(Power = scales::percent(pw), `Required participants` = ceiling(out$n))
})
power_rows |> knitr::kable(caption = sprintf(
  "Original-code planning approximation: one-sample two-sided t-test, alpha=.05, absolute Cohen d=%.4f, based on original Exp1 unchosen proportions (N=%d). Not a direct power calculation for the Bayesian hierarchical model.",
  original_d, original_summary$unchosen_subject_n))
# Compatibility for the template's inline expressions; student must replace
# its obsolete gain/loss prose. This within-person design has ONE sample N.
two_and_half <- ceiling(2.5 * original_n)
```

For comparison, 2.5 times the original sample would be 308 (rounded up from 307.5) usable participants in total.

### Planned sample

The experiment will recruit U.S. residents aged 18-35 who are fluent in English through Prolific. Participants must complete the experiment on a computer with a keyboard. Those who fail to respond on three timed practice trials or do not complete the experiment will be excluded. Participants are also excluded if accuracy on the letter attention checks is below 10% or if the nonresponse rate is above 90%. Data collection will continue until 118 participants pass the exclusion criteria, providing approximately 80% power.

### Materials

Wang et al. (2026) described the stimuli as follows:

> “The image stimuli were taken from the DinoLab Object Database” (p. 2, §2.2).

> “128 images of common objects from 8 semantic categories (16 objects per category): land mammals, ocean creatures, vegetables, fruits, sports, vehicles, musical instruments, and buildings.” (p. 2, §2.2).

The replication uses the same set of stimuli downloaded from the DinoLab Object Database, with one substitution: an image of a cinnamon bun was replaced with an image of a shrimp in the ocean creatures category.

[Stimulus files](https://github.com/psych251/wang2026/tree/main/stimuli)

### Procedure

1.  Consent and introduction: Participants provide Stanford course consent and receive instructions to build a valuable stamp portfolio by selecting pictures. Adaptation: Course consent and reconstructed instructions based on original instructions for better clarity.

2.  Pre-experimental phase: Participants rate 24 randomized pictures (three from each of eight categories) “based on their personal preferences” using a slide bar on a 0-100 scale.

3.  Deliberation phase: Participants “choose the images they predicted would be placed on the most valuable stamp” across four pairs repeated in two practice rounds and one final round (12 choices in total). Participants press J to choose the left option and K to choose the right option. Practice choices are timed (5s), while final choices are untimed. The second practice round requires written justifications for their choices. Three missed practice responses terminate the session.

4.  Choice Outcome phase: Four chosen pictures receive randomly assigned outcomes (two rewarded, two unrewarded), with pictures shown alone for 1 s followed by “reward or no reward” for 2 s with pictures. Unchosen pictures receive no feedback.

5.  Final Decision phase: Participants make 48 choices (24 chosen-category and 24 unchosen-category pairs) using six new pictures per category, each presented twice. Participants need to press keys shown on the screen to pass occasional attention checks.

6.  Surprise Memory phase: Participants respond to eight old/new recognition trials (four chosen and four unseen pictures; 1 = old, 0 = new). When an original picture is correctly recognized, participants need to choose its paired partner from four options.

7.  Optional final questions: Participants answer demographic, instruction-clarity, and feedback questions. Adaptation: Course-template questions.

8.  Debrief and completion: Participants learn the study purpose and that outcomes were randomly assigned and complete submitting their responses. Adaptation: Course-specific debrief.

Participants are expected to finish the entire experiment in 10-20 minutes.

### Analysis plan

**Key analysis of interest.** Participants are predicted to prefer novel items from unchosen categories whose chosen counterparts received no reward, than those whose counterparts were rewarded. It will be tested using a multilevel Bayesian logistic regression on the 24 unchosen-category decisions per participant, controlling for initial category preferences and including a random intercept for each participant. The effect size will be reported as an odds ratio with a 95% credible interval.

**Secondary confirmatory and exploratory analyses.** Secondary confirmatory analyses will use multilevel Bayesian logistic regressions for chosen-category decisions and for chosen- and unchosen-category decisions combined. Exploratory follow-up analyses may include the original study’s Bayesian multilevel analyses of RT and adaptive choice, descriptive memory summaries, and memory–choice analyses using Spearman correlations and permutation tests.

**Exclusions.** Participants are excluded if they fail to respond on three timed practice trials or do not complete the study. Participants are also excluded if accuracy on the letter attention checks is below 10% or if the nonresponse rate is above 90%. Both rates use all presented attention checks, and nonresponses count as incorrect. Participants with no presented attention checks are not excluded on this basis.

### Differences from the original study

| Aspect | Original study | This replication | Expected to matter? |
|------------------|-------------------|------------------|------------------|
| Sample | University of Chicago SONA and MTurk/CloudResearch | Prolific | Unlikely. Participants will be recruited using the same eligibility criteria. |
| Stimuli | Ocean creatures category includes a cinnamon bun | Replaced the cinnamon bun with a shrimp | Unlikely. The replacement better matches the intended semantic category. |
| Instructions | Long paragraphs in the original SVG instructions | Reconstructed shorter phase-specific instructions for better clarity, with typos corrected | Unlikely though there is a chance differences in wording could affect how participants understand the task. |
| Exclusions | Three missed timed Deliberation responses or incompletion | Same criteria, plus letter attention-check accuracy below 10% or nonresponse rate above 90%, following the original analysis code (although these criteria were not reported for Experiment 1 in the paper) | Unlikely. Unattended participants were also excluded from the original Experiment 2. |

#| label: demographics

demo <- trials |>
  filter(task == "demographics", participant_id %in% keep$participant_id) |>
  mutate(resp = map(response, ~ fromJSON(.x))) |>
  transmute(
    participant_id,
    age    = map_dbl(resp, ~ as.numeric(.x$age %||% NA)),
    gender = map_chr(resp, ~ as.character(.x$gender %||% NA))

if (nrow(demo) > 0) {
  demo |>
    summarise(N = n(), `Mean age` = round(mean(age, na.rm = TRUE), 1),
              `SD age` = round(sd(age, na.rm = TRUE), 1),
              `Age not given` = sum(is.na(age))) |>
    knitr::kable(caption = "Age of the analysed sample.")
}

### Data preparation

Data preparation follows the analysis plan. Loading and exclusions are done by the shared analysis code under Key statistics (open "Show the analysis code"). Describe anything you did to the data beyond that.

### Confirmatory analysis

#### Primary analysis

```{r}
#| label: confirmatory
#| eval: !expr have_data
#| results: asis
# The primary model matches the Introduction and Methods: unchosen trials only.
# Chosen and combined models are reported below as secondary analyses.
if (!is.null(phase1_fits)) {
  primary_fit <- phase1_fits$unchosen
  cat("```text\n")
  print(primary_fit, digits = 3)
  cat("\n```\n\n")
  primary_fixed <- rstanarm::fixef(primary_fit)
  primary_table <- map_dfr(names(primary_fixed), function(term)
    or_summary(primary_fit, term) |> mutate(Term = term)) |>
    select(Term, everything())
  cat(knitr::kable(primary_table, digits = 3,
    caption = "Primary confirmatory analysis: unchosen-category model, adjusted for the source-code rating covariate. Intercept OR below 1 is the predicted inverse preference."), sep = "\n")
  cat("\n\n")
  cat(knitr::kable(diagnostics(phase1_fits["unchosen"]), digits = 3,
    caption = "MCMC diagnostics for the primary unchosen-category model."), sep = "\n")
  cat("\n\n")
}
```

#### Secondary analyses

```{r}
#| eval: !expr have_data
#| results: asis
# Reuse the already fitted models; no extra model fitting or exclusions.
if (!is.null(phase1_fits)) {
  secondary_models <- list(`Chosen-category model` = phase1_fits$chosen,
                          `Combined model` = phase1_fits$main)
  for (model_name in names(secondary_models)) {
    fit <- secondary_models[[model_name]]
    secondary_table <- map_dfr(names(rstanarm::fixef(fit)), function(term)
      or_summary(fit, term) |> mutate(Term = term)) |>
      select(Term, everything())
    cat(knitr::kable(secondary_table, digits = 3,
      caption = paste0("Secondary confirmatory analysis: ", model_name,
        if (model_name == "Combined model")
          ". Trial type is coded chosen = 0, unchosen = 1; the model includes the rating covariate and its interaction with trial type."
        else ". Adjusted for the source-code rating covariate.")), sep = "\n")
    cat("\n\n")
  }
  cat(knitr::kable(diagnostics(secondary_models), digits = 3,
    caption = "MCMC diagnostics for the secondary chosen-category and combined models."), sep = "\n")
  cat("\n\n")
}
```

### Replication assessment

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Guidance

Judge the replication on effect sizes, not only on whether the key test is significant. Compare the replication estimate and its interval with the original: does the interval exclude zero, and does it include the original estimate? A significant result much smaller than the original, or a non-significant result whose interval still includes the original effect, are both informative and should be reported as such (Experimentology §3.2).
:::

```{r}
#| label: comparison
#| eval: !expr have_data
bind_rows(original |> mutate(Study = "Original: Exp1"),
          phase1_estimates |> mutate(Study = "Phase 1: replication (Pilot B)")) |>
  filter(pair_type == "unchosen") |>
  transmute(Study, `Pair type` = pair_type, N, OR = round(odds_ratio, 3),
            `95% HPDI` = format_hpdi(lower, upper)) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Primary unchosen-category model intercept: original published OR and Pilot B posterior median OR, with 95% HPD intervals. The chosen and combined models are secondary and do not determine the replication assessment.")
```

```{r}
#| label: comparison-verdict
#| eval: !expr have_data
#| echo: false
if (nrow(phase1_estimates)) phase1_estimates |>
  filter(pair_type == "unchosen") |>
  transmute(`Predicted direction (OR<1)` = odds_ratio < 1,
    `95% HPDI below1` = upper < 1,
    `95% HPDI includes original0.69` = lower <= 0.69 & upper >= 0.69) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Pilot diagnostics only; the small Pilot B sample does not establish a replication outcome.")
```

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Guidance: show the original next to your replication

**Every report should have a figure that puts the original finding and your replication side by side.** It is the single most informative thing in a replication report: a reader can see at a glance whether the effect came back, and how its size compares. Make it however you can, in roughly this order of preference:

1.  **Replot both from numbers.** Enter the original's summary statistics (means or proportions, with SDs, SEs or CIs, and Ns) in the original-study chunk at the top of this file, and plot them on the same axes as yours. That is what the demo figure below does.

2.  **Replot the original from its data**, if the authors shared it or it is in an open repository, using exactly the same plotting code as for your own data.

3.  **Show the original figure as an image** next to yours if neither is possible. Save a screenshot of it, for example as `writeup/images/original-figure.png`, and lay the two out in columns:

    ```` markdown
    ::: {layout-ncol=2}
    ![Original: Tversky & Kahneman (1981), Figure 1](images/original-figure.png)

    ```{{r}}
    # your replication plot here
    ```
    :::
    ````

Whichever you choose, use the same measure, scale, condition order and error-bar meaning for both panels, label which is which, and cite the source of the original values or figure in the caption. If the original reported no variability, say so rather than leaving it out silently.
:::

```{r}
#| label: fig-comparison
#| eval: !expr have_data
#| fig-cap: "Primary unchosen-category effect in original Experiment 1 (Wang et al., 2026, section 3.2) and Pilot B. Points are model-intercept odds ratios for choosing NS+; bars are 95% HPD intervals on log odds, exponentiated. Original points use published estimates; pilot points use posterior medians. Both panels use the same scale. The dashed line is OR = 1. Pilot B checks the pipeline and does not establish a final replication outcome."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4
comparison_plot(`Original: Exp1` = filter(original, pair_type == "unchosen"),
                `Pilot B` = filter(phase1_estimates, pair_type == "unchosen"))
```

### Exploratory analyses

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Guidance

Any follow-up analyses (optional). Label them clearly as exploratory: they were not planned, so they generate hypotheses rather than test them.
:::

```{r}
#| label: exploratory-rt
#| eval: !expr have_data
#| cache: true
#| cache.extra: !expr list(id = experiment_id, hashes = tools::md5sum(analysis_input_files[file.exists(analysis_input_files)]), rstanarm = as.character(packageVersion("rstanarm")))
#| results: asis
# Wang et al. (2026), sections 2.4.3–2.4.4; OSF xjhkf,
# Experiment_1_analysis.Rmd: RT models (1194–1217, 1354–1374), memory
# scoring (1690–1745, 1913–1920), corrected correlations (2141–2217).
# No extra source-Rmd supplementary regressions are added here.
prepare_exploratory_choices <- function(d) {
  # These models have no initial-preference covariate: a missing rating does
  # not discard an otherwise usable RT/choice. Participant exclusions persist.
  d$choices |>
    filter(pair_type %in% c("chosen", "unchosen"), !timed_out,
           !is.na(p_ns), is.finite(rt), rt > 0) |>
    mutate(pid = factor(participant_id),
           trial_type = as.integer(pair_type == "unchosen"),
           adaptive = if_else(pair_type == "chosen", p_ns, 1L - p_ns)) |>
    group_by(participant_id) |>
    mutate(z_rt = if (n() > 1L && sd(rt) > 0) as.numeric(scale(rt)) else NA_real_) |>
    ungroup()
}
score_exploratory_memory <- function(d) {
  items <- d$retained |> filter(task == "item_memory") |>
    mutate(old = as_bool(is_old), recognized = as_bool(responded_old))
  associations <- d$retained |> filter(task == "associative_memory") |>
    select(participant_id, memory_id, response, option_roles)
  # Match by explicit memory ID, not adjacent trial indices or row order.
  stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(items[c("participant_id", "memory_id")]),
            !anyDuplicated(associations[c("participant_id", "memory_id")]))
  selected_role <- function(response, roles) {
    index <- suppressWarnings(as.integer(response))
    if (is.na(index)) return(NA_character_) # Timed-out pairing: no credit.
    options <- jsonlite::fromJSON(roles)
    stopifnot(index >= 1L, index <= length(options))
    options[[index]]
  }
  associations <- associations |>
    mutate(role = map2_chr(response, option_roles, selected_role),
           association_present = TRUE)
  scored <- items |> filter(old) |>
    left_join(associations, by = c("participant_id", "memory_id"),
              suffix = c("", "_association"))
  # A recognized cue must have its conditional pairing record. Missing export
  # records are not silently converted to errors or fabricated responses.
  stopifnot(all(!scored$recognized | !is.na(scored$association_present)))
  scored <- scored |>
    mutate(category_credit = recognized & coalesce(role %in% c("target", "same_category_lure"), FALSE),
           item_credit = recognized & coalesce(role == "target", FALSE),
           points = as.integer(recognized) + as.integer(category_credit) + as.integer(item_credit))
  old_scores <- scored |> group_by(participant_id) |>
    summarise(old_trials = n(), raw_memory = mean(points) / 3, .groups = "drop")
  foils <- items |> filter(!old) |> group_by(participant_id) |>
    summarise(foil_trials = n(), false_alarm_rate = mean(recognized), .groups = "drop")
  old_scores |> full_join(foils, by = "participant_id") |>
    mutate(corrected_memory = if_else(old_trials == 4L & foil_trials == 4L,
                                      raw_memory - false_alarm_rate, NA_real_))
}
safe_spearman <- function(x, y) {
  if (length(x) < 3L || n_distinct(x) < 2L || n_distinct(y) < 2L) return(NA_real_)
  unname(cor(x, y, method = "spearman"))
}
spearman_permutation <- function(x, y, B = 10000L, seed = 123L) {
  valid <- is.finite(x) & is.finite(y)
  x <- x[valid]; y <- y[valid]
  observed <- safe_spearman(x, y)
  if (!is.finite(observed)) return(tibble(N = length(x), rho = NA_real_,
    `Permutation p (two-sided)` = NA_real_, `Valid permutations` = 0L,
    Status = "Not estimable: fewer than 3 complete pairs or no variation"))
  set.seed(seed)
  # Permuting participant-level outcomes preserves tied ranks. No extra
  # package is needed for the authors' rank-based Monte Carlo test.
  null <- replicate(B, safe_spearman(x, sample(y)))
  tibble(N = length(x), rho = observed,
    `Permutation p (two-sided)` = (1 + sum(abs(null) >= abs(observed) - 1e-12)) / (B + 1),
    `Valid permutations` = B, Status = "Exploratory")
}
memory_correlation_difference <- function(d, B = 10000L, seed = 123L) {
  # Reproduce the authors' pooled group-label shuffle (not a within-person
  # swap test). Each retained participant contributes one row per trial type.
  wide <- d |> filter(is.finite(corrected_memory), is.finite(adaptive_proportion)) |>
    select(participant_id, corrected_memory, pair_type, adaptive_proportion) |>
    pivot_wider(names_from = pair_type, values_from = adaptive_proportion)
  if (!"chosen" %in% names(wide)) wide$chosen <- NA_real_
  if (!"unchosen" %in% names(wide)) wide$unchosen <- NA_real_
  wide <- wide |> filter(is.finite(chosen), is.finite(unchosen))
  observed <- safe_spearman(wide$corrected_memory, wide$chosen) -
    safe_spearman(wide$corrected_memory, wide$unchosen)
  if (!is.finite(observed)) return(tibble(N = nrow(wide),
    `rho chosen minus unchosen` = NA_real_, `Permutation p (two-sided)` = NA_real_,
    `Valid permutations` = 0L, Status = "Not estimable: insufficient pairs or no variation"))
  x <- rep(wide$corrected_memory, 2L)
  y <- c(wide$chosen, wide$unchosen)
  group <- rep(c(TRUE, FALSE), each = nrow(wide))
  set.seed(seed)
  null <- replicate(B, {
    shuffled <- sample(group)
    safe_spearman(x[shuffled], y[shuffled]) - safe_spearman(x[!shuffled], y[!shuffled])
  })
  valid <- is.finite(null)
  tibble(N = nrow(wide), `rho chosen minus unchosen` = observed,
    `Permutation p (two-sided)` = if (any(valid))
      (1 + sum(abs(null[valid]) >= abs(observed) - 1e-12)) / (1 + sum(valid)) else NA_real_,
    `Valid permutations` = sum(valid),
    Status = if (all(valid)) "Exploratory: authors' pooled-label shuffle" else
      "Exploratory: undefined permutations omitted; inspect small-sample limitations")
}
fit_exploratory_rt <- function(x) {
  if (n_distinct(x$pid) < 2L || n_distinct(x$trial_type) < 2L) return(list())
  # Source RT model uses default fixed-effect/intercept/auxiliary priors;
  # source RT-choice model explicitly uses normal(0, 2.5). Preserve that
  # distinction instead of borrowing logistic priors for raw RT in ms.
  rt_fit <- rstanarm::stan_glmer(rt ~ trial_type + (1 | pid), data = x,
    family = inverse.gaussian(link = "log"),
    prior_covariance = rstanarm::decov(regularization = 1),
    chains = 4, iter = 4000, warmup = 2000, seed = 123, refresh = 0)
  sampler <- rstan::get_sampler_params(rt_fit$stanfit, inc_warmup = FALSE)
  if (sum(vapply(sampler, function(s) sum(s[, "divergent__"]), numeric(1))) > 0) {
    rt_fit <- update(rt_fit, adapt_delta = 0.99, refresh = 0)
    attr(rt_fit, "tolerance_tightened") <- TRUE
  }
  fits <- list(`RT by trial type` = rt_fit)
  choice_data <- x |> filter(is.finite(z_rt))
  if (n_distinct(choice_data$pid) >= 2L && n_distinct(choice_data$trial_type) == 2L &&
      n_distinct(choice_data$adaptive) == 2L) {
    fits[["Adaptive choice by RT"]] <- fit_source_model(choice_data,
      adaptive ~ trial_type * z_rt + (1 | pid))
  }
  fits
}
exploratory_fixed_effects <- function(fits) {
  imap_dfr(fits, function(fit, model) {
    map_dfr(names(rstanarm::fixef(fit)), function(term) {
      draws <- as.matrix(fit)[, term]
      hpdi <- coda::HPDinterval(coda::mcmc(draws), prob = 0.95)[1, ]
      tibble(Model = model, Term = term, `Log coefficient` = median(draws),
        `95% HPDI lower (log)` = hpdi[1], `95% HPDI upper (log)` = hpdi[2],
        `Exponentiated coefficient` = exp(median(draws)),
        `95% HPDI lower (exp)` = exp(hpdi[1]), `95% HPDI upper (exp)` = exp(hpdi[2]))
    })
  })
}
exploratory_diagnostic_status <- function(fits) {
  diagnostics(fits) |>
    mutate(`Estimates reportable` = is.finite(`Maximum Rhat`) & `Maximum Rhat` <= 1.01 &
             is.finite(`Minimum effective N`) & `Minimum effective N` >= 400 & Divergences == 0L)
}
show_exploratory_table <- function(x, caption, digits = 3) {
  cat(knitr::kable(x, digits = digits, caption = caption), sep = "\n")
  cat("\n\n")
}
exploratory_choices <- prepare_exploratory_choices(phase1)
exploratory_memory <- score_exploratory_memory(phase1)
exploratory_rt_fits <- fit_exploratory_rt(exploratory_choices)
show_exploratory_table(
  exploratory_choices |> group_by(pair_type) |>
    summarise(N = n_distinct(participant_id), Trials = n(),
      `Mean RT (ms)` = mean(rt), `SD RT (ms)` = sd(rt), .groups = "drop"),
  "Exploratory final-choice RTs: responded trials with finite, positive RT; no additional trimming.", 1)
if (length(exploratory_rt_fits)) {
  exploratory_diagnostics <- exploratory_diagnostic_status(exploratory_rt_fits)
  reportable_models <- exploratory_diagnostics$Model[exploratory_diagnostics$`Estimates reportable`]
  withheld_models <- exploratory_diagnostics$Model[!exploratory_diagnostics$`Estimates reportable`]
  if (length(reportable_models)) show_exploratory_table(
    exploratory_fixed_effects(exploratory_rt_fits[reportable_models]),
    "Exploratory Bayesian RT models. Exponentiated RT slopes are RT ratios; the exponentiated RT intercept is baseline RT in milliseconds. Exponentiated logistic coefficients are odds ratios for adaptive choice. Trial type: chosen = 0, unchosen = 1; RT z-scores are within participant.")
  if (length(withheld_models)) cat(paste0(
    "Estimates withheld because sampler diagnostics failed: ",
    paste(withheld_models, collapse = ", "),
    ". The source model and priors are retained; no substitute model was fitted.\n\n"))
  show_exploratory_table(exploratory_diagnostics,
    paste0("MCMC diagnostics for exploratory models (N = ",
      n_distinct(exploratory_choices$participant_id),
      "). Estimates require maximum Rhat <= 1.01, minimum effective N >= 400 and zero divergences. Pilot estimates check the pipeline and do not establish final-sample effects."))
  if (!"Adaptive choice by RT" %in% names(exploratory_rt_fits))
    cat("Adaptive-choice RT model not estimable: insufficient participants, trial types, RT variation, or outcome variation.\n\n")
} else {
  cat("Exploratory RT models not estimable: fewer than two participants or missing trial-type variation.\n\n")
}
memory_checks <- phase1$retained |> filter(task == "item_memory") |>
  group_by(participant_id) |> summarise(item_accuracy = mean(as_bool(correct)), .groups = "drop")
association_checks <- phase1$retained |> filter(task == "associative_memory") |>
  group_by(participant_id) |> summarise(association_accuracy = mean(as_bool(correct)), .groups = "drop")
show_exploratory_table(
  memory_checks |> left_join(association_checks, by = "participant_id") |>
    left_join(exploratory_memory, by = "participant_id") |>
    summarise(N = n(), `Mean item accuracy` = mean(item_accuracy),
      `Mean conditional association accuracy` = mean(association_accuracy, na.rm = TRUE),
      `N with complete corrected score` = sum(is.finite(corrected_memory)),
      `Mean corrected memory score` = mean(corrected_memory, na.rm = TRUE)),
  "Memory checks and corrected score. Association accuracy is conditional on recognizing the original chosen cue; the corrected score includes all four old cues, then subtracts the false-alarm rate across four novel items.")
# Match source aggregation over responded positive-RT trials; the same
# participant memory score is related separately to chosen/unchosen choices.
memory_choice <- exploratory_choices |> group_by(participant_id, pair_type) |>
  summarise(adaptive_proportion = mean(adaptive), .groups = "drop") |>
  left_join(exploratory_memory, by = "participant_id")
memory_correlations <- map_dfr(c("chosen", "unchosen"), function(type) {
  d <- memory_choice |> filter(pair_type == type)
  spearman_permutation(d$corrected_memory, d$adaptive_proportion) |>
    mutate(`Pair type` = type, .before = 1)
})
show_exploratory_table(memory_correlations,
  "Exploratory corrected-memory versus adaptive-choice Spearman correlations. Two-sided participant-outcome permutation tests: 10,000 shuffles, seed 123, plus-one correction; participants need a complete memory score.")
show_exploratory_table(memory_correlation_difference(memory_choice),
  "Exploratory difference in Spearman correlations (chosen minus unchosen), using the authors' pooled trial-type-label shuffle over complete participant pairs: 10,000 permutations, seed 123, two-sided plus-one correction. This reproduces their pooled-label procedure rather than a paired within-participant swap test.")
```

## Discussion

### Summary of replication attempt

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Guidance

Open with one paragraph summarizing the result of the key analysis and your assessment of whether the original finding replicated, partially replicated, or failed to replicate. Base that judgment on the replication assessment above: the size of the effect relative to the original, not just the p value.
:::

### Commentary

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Guidance

Open-ended commentary, none of it long: (a) what the exploratory analyses suggest; (b) what the replication means, for example whether the differences between your study and the original are definitely, plausibly, or unlikely to be moderators of the result; and (c) any objections or challenges raised by you or the original authors.
:::

# Phase 2: Extension

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Guidance: choosing your extension

Follow the Extension guidelines page on Canvas. In brief:

- **By default the extension is a best-practices modification of your Phase 1 experiment.** If your replication did not succeed, it is a **rescue**: address the plausible reasons for the failure. If it did succeed, it is an **upgrade**: make the estimate more precise. Typical changes are better or more reliable measurement, more trials, a within-participant design where that is legitimate, comprehension and manipulation checks, clearer instructions, or a larger or better-targeted sample.
- **If your scientific extension pitch was approved at Milestone 3 and your replication succeeded, propose that instead:** the original conditions rerun unchanged, plus the one added condition or manipulation, with a power analysis for the new comparison.
- On either track you may add exploratory measures **at the end** of the study.
- Every change is listed and tagged by category below; everything else stays identical.

State your track on the line below, and delete the others.
:::

**Track:** Best-practices upgrade / Best-practices rescue / Scientific extension (approved at Milestone 3)

## Rationale

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Guidance

One or two paragraphs. For a rescue: what are the plausible reasons Phase 1 did not reproduce the original result, and how does each change address one of them? For an upgrade: where is the Phase 1 estimate least precise or least trustworthy, and how will the changes improve it? For a scientific extension: what question does the added condition answer, and why does it follow from the original finding?
:::

## Changes from Phase 1

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Guidance

Every change from the Phase 1 experiment, one per row, each tagged with a category: Measurement, Trials, Design, Checks, Instructions, Sample, Added condition (scientific track only), or Exploratory measure (end of study only). If it is not in this table, it does not change: same materials, wording, procedure, exclusion rule and analysis. The rows below are examples for the demo; replace them with yours.
:::

| \# | Category | Phase 1 | Phase 2 | Why |
|---------------|---------------|---------------|---------------|---------------|
| 1 | Sample | 27 analysed participants | 300 analysed participants (150 per frame) | Phase 1's interval was too wide to distinguish the original effect from a much smaller one. |
| 2 | Checks | No comprehension check | After the choice, participants say how many people are at risk (600) | Confirms participants read the scenario; failures are reported, and excluded only if preregistered. |
| 3 | Exploratory measure | None | At the end: "How confident are you in your choice?" (1–7) | Exploratory only; collected after every confirmatory measure. |

Everything not listed above is identical to Phase 1.

## Power and sample

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Guidance

Justify the Phase 2 sample, and **state how you expect the estimate and its precision to compare with Phase 1**. For an upgrade, plan the sample around the confidence interval you want; for a rescue, around the power to detect the original effect, or the smallest effect you would still consider a successful replication; for a scientific extension, around the power to detect the new comparison. Set `phase2_n_per_group` in the code below; the table uses Phase 1's estimate if you have it and the original's otherwise.
:::

```{r}
#| label: phase2-power
# Phase2 design/sample have not been selected. Do not retain the demo's
# invented150-per-group plan or power based on a three-person pilot effect.
phase2_planned_n <- NA_integer_
tibble(`Phase2 planned N` = phase2_planned_n) |> knitr::kable(na = "Not specified")
```

## Analysis plan

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Guidance

The confirmatory analysis for Phase 2, written before Phase 2 data collection. On the best-practices tracks this is normally the same key test as Phase 1, run on the Phase 2 data alone; say whether you will also report a pooled estimate across phases, and label it exploratory if so. On the scientific track, specify the test for the new comparison. Name the exclusion rule (unchanged unless it is in the Changes table) and list any exploratory measures.

Run Phase 2 under a new `EXPERIMENT.id` in `experiment.js` (for example `smith2016-phase2`) and set `experiment_id_phase2` at the top of this file to match, so the two phases' data never mix.
:::
